summary:
I developed Ground Movement Near Infrastructure, an interactive web map that uses NASA-ISRO NISAR radar to show where the ground is moving under roads, buildings, and rail lines, and by how much.

It addresses the challenge by tracking two kinds of surface change in two countries. At the Portuguese Bend landslide in California, about 2 km² moved at least 57 cm in 11 months, under 222 mapped buildings. In Mexico City, about 73 km² sank about 16 cm in a year, under metro lines and runways. Users can play through the dates, click any point for a measurement, and compare two satellite viewing directions.

It matters because slow ground movement damages infrastructure long before anyone sees it, and engineers cannot put sensors everywhere. This map shows where to look first. It also states its own limits and lists what an engineer would check on the ground, because a map people act on has to be honest.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Ground Movement Near Infrastructure is an interactive web map that shows where the ground is moving under roads, buildings, and rail lines, and by how much. It uses radar from the NASA-ISRO NISAR satellite and covers two places with two kinds of surface change: the Portuguese Bend landslide in California and sinking ground in Mexico City.

A user picks a place, steps through the dates with a slider or a Play button, and clicks anywhere to read the movement in centimeters. They can switch between two satellite viewing directions, show the total of all dates as one map, and see a chart of how the moving area changed over time. The moving area is outlined, along with the infrastructure that crosses it.

HOW IT WORKS

1. In Google Colab, each NISAR interferogram is opened over the internet and only the pixels over the sites are read, so the multi-gigabyte files are never downloaded.

2. Low-quality pixels are hidden (coherence below 0.3, or where phase unwrapping failed).

3. Radar phase is converted to displacement: displacement = -(wavelength / 4 pi) x phase, using NISAR's 24.2 cm wavelength.

4. Each date pair is measured against the typical pixel in the map area, because this kind of radar measurement is relative.

5. Each moving area is defined from all the dates together, not from one pair.

6. One data file per place is exported. A static web page draws the map, chart, and outlines in the browser.

WHAT I FOUND

Portuguese Bend: about 2 km2 moved away from the satellite in all 25 date pairs from November 2025 to October 2026, at least 57 cm in total along the radar's line of sight. 222 mapped buildings and Palos Verdes Drive South sit on it.

Mexico City: about 73 km2 east of the city center sank about 16 cm in a year. The two viewing directions gave about 16 cm and 15 cm. Sinking is straight down, so the two views should agree, and they do. Metro lines, major roads, and runways cross the area.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Roads, pipes, foundations, and rail lines all depend on the ground staying put, and slow movement is invisible until something cracks. Engineers and cities cannot put sensors everywhere. This project shows them where to look first, and which structures are on the moving ground, using free public data.

TOOLS

Python in Google Colab (earthaccess, h5py, NumPy, SciPy, pyproj) for the data processing. HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with the Leaflet map library for the app. OpenStreetMap for buildings, roads, and rail lines. GitHub Pages for hosting. Code: https://github.com/shadowbrokers2390/nasa-space-apps

AI acknowledgment: the code and the draft of this text were written with Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant, working under my direction. This is labeled in every code and data file and in the app. The measurements come from NISAR data, not from an AI model.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

It connects movement to what is built on it, naming the buildings, roads, and rail lines, instead of only showing a colored map. It uses two viewing directions as a check: a landslide moving sideways looks different from each side, while sinking looks the same from both. It pairs the satellite view with ground instruments, listing what an engineer would install to confirm each result.

WHAT I CONSIDERED

Honesty about limits: the data is Provisional, radar measures motion only toward or away from the satellite, and fast-moving ground can be underestimated, so every number is "at least". The app says this on screen.

Not overclaiming: "on the moving area" does not mean "damaged", and the data does not prove a cause.

Leaving out what I could not trust: I also processed California's Central Valley. No sinking patch there was consistent between dates or between viewing directions, so it is not in the app.

Before the event I explored NISAR data for Portuguese Bend to learn how it works. The project submitted here was built during the event.
